conversation.content: We need to design a real-time chat system — think WhatsApp or Slack. Both 1:1 and group messaging. Take it from the top.

Let me scope this. Key questions: how many concurrent users? Maximum group size? Do we need message persistence, or ephemeral only? What about end-to-end encryption? Media support — images, files? Read receipts, typing indicators? And what's our delivery guarantee — at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once?
50 million concurrent connections. Groups up to 500 members. Persistent messages. No E2E encryption for now. Images and files yes. Read receipts and typing indicators yes. At-least-once delivery. Go.

For the connection layer, I'd use WebSockets. Each client maintains a persistent WebSocket connection to a chat server. This gives us real-time bidirectional communication with low overhead after the initial handshake. At 50M concurrent connections, if each server handles 50K connections, we need about 1,000 WebSocket servers.

Why WebSocket? Long polling is simpler to operate — no persistent connection state, works through every proxy and load balancer, no connection management headaches. Why wouldn't you just use long polling?

Long polling has fundamental problems for this use case. First, latency: with long polling, there's an inherent delay between when a message is available and when the next poll picks it up, plus the overhead of re-establishing HTTP connections constantly. For a chat app, users expect sub-100ms delivery — long polling typically gives you 100-500ms. Second, server load: 50 million users each polling every few seconds generates enormous request volume, each with full HTTP headers. WebSocket has a one-time handshake cost, then tiny frames. Third, bidirectional — typing indicators and read receipts need server-to-client push. With long polling you need a separate mechanism. That said, you're right about operability — WebSocket requires sticky sessions or a connection registry, and some corporate proxies terminate them. I'd use WebSocket as primary with long polling as a fallback for hostile network environments.
Fair. Now, you said 1,000 WebSocket servers. How does Server A know that User B is connected to Server C when User A sends a message to User B?

We need a connection registry — a mapping of user_id to the server they're connected to. I'd store this in Redis. When a user connects, the WebSocket server registers the mapping. When a message needs to be delivered, the sending server looks up the recipient's server in Redis and forwards the message. For group messages, we look up all group members' servers and fan out to each. The registry needs to handle disconnects and reconnects — we'd use Redis key expiration with heartbeat refreshes.

But now you've created a chatty internal network. Server A sends a group message to a 500-person group — that could mean 500 lookups and potentially 500 different servers to forward to. Why not use a pub/sub system instead? Each server subscribes to relevant channels.

You're right that direct server-to-server forwarding gets messy at scale. A pub/sub layer is cleaner. Each group gets a channel. When a user connects to a WebSocket server, that server subscribes to all channels for the user's groups. Message goes to the channel, and all subscribed servers receive it and push to their connected clients. Redis Pub/Sub could work, but at 50M users it won't scale — Redis Pub/Sub is single-threaded per node. I'd use Kafka or NATS instead. Kafka gives us persistence and replay — important for at-least-once delivery. NATS is faster but ephemeral. Given our delivery guarantee, I'd go with Kafka for message routing between servers.

Kafka for real-time chat? Kafka has high throughput but its latency is measured in tens of milliseconds minimum. You said users expect sub-100ms. Isn't NATS better for this exact use case — microsecond-level pub/sub?

You're making a good point, and I think the answer is actually both. Let me revise: NATS for the real-time delivery path — when a message comes in, it's published to NATS for immediate push to connected clients. Kafka for the durable path — the message is also written to Kafka for persistence, offline delivery, and replay. If a user is online, they get the message via NATS in microseconds. If they're offline or the NATS delivery fails, the Kafka consumer handles it when they reconnect. This dual-write pattern is more complex but gives us both low latency and durability.

Dual-write means you can have messages delivered out of order or duplicated. User sends 'Hello' then 'World' — one arrives via NATS, the other via Kafka catch-up. Now they see 'World' then 'Hello'. How do you handle ordering?

Each message gets a server-assigned sequence number scoped to the conversation. When we first receive the message, we assign it a monotonically increasing sequence number for that conversation — stored in Redis with INCR or in the database. Both the NATS path and the Kafka path carry this sequence number. The client maintains a local buffer and reorders messages by sequence number before displaying. If message 5 arrives before message 4, the client waits briefly — say 200ms — and if 4 doesn't arrive, it requests it explicitly. For the dual delivery, the client also deduplicates using the message ID. So even if a message arrives via both paths, the user sees it once, in order.
That sequence number assignment is a single point of contention per conversation. A busy group chat with 500 members — that's a lot of INCR operations on one key. Isn't that a bottleneck?

In practice, no. Redis INCR is O(1) and handles millions of operations per second on a single key. Even the busiest group chat won't generate more than a few hundred messages per second. The contention point is the network round trip to Redis for the INCR, which adds 0.5-1ms per message. If even that's too much, we could batch — the app server reserves a range of 100 sequence numbers and assigns locally, similar to the ID generation pattern we see in other systems. But honestly, a single INCR per message at the volumes we're talking about is a non-issue. The real contention would be if we were using a database instead of Redis.
Alright, I'll accept that. What about message storage? You said persistent messages. SQL or NoSQL?

I'd go with Cassandra. The access pattern is write-heavy and append-only — new messages are always written, rarely updated. Reads are primarily sequential — load messages in a conversation sorted by time. Cassandra's LSM-tree storage engine excels at this: fast writes and efficient range scans. Partition key would be conversation_id, clustering key would be the sequence number. This ensures all messages in a conversation are colocated on the same partition for efficient reads. With a replication factor of 3 across multiple racks, we get durability without a separate replication layer.
Cassandra has no transactions. What if you need to update the conversation's 'last_message' preview and write the message atomically? PostgreSQL gives you that for free.

True — Cassandra trades transactions for scale. For the last_message preview, I'd handle it differently: the conversation metadata (last message, unread count, etc.) lives in a separate store — Redis or even PostgreSQL if we want transactions there. The message table in Cassandra is the source of truth for message content. The conversation metadata store is updated asynchronously — a slight delay in the preview is acceptable. If the metadata update fails, the next message or a periodic reconciliation job fixes it. We're using eventual consistency where it's tolerable and reserving strong consistency for where it matters — which is message ordering and delivery, not conversation previews.
Now you have three data stores — Redis, Cassandra, and maybe PostgreSQL for metadata. Isn't that operational nightmare territory? Three systems to monitor, back up, scale, and keep consistent.

It's a valid concern, and this is a real tradeoff at principal-level design. We could simplify: drop PostgreSQL and put conversation metadata in Cassandra too, using a separate table with conversation_id as partition key. That's two systems instead of three. Redis is non-negotiable — we need it for connection state, sequence numbers, and presence. Cassandra handles all persistent data. Alternatively, we could go all-in on PostgreSQL with Citus for sharding and skip Cassandra — Citus handles both the transactional and the append-heavy workloads reasonably well. The choice depends on the team's operational expertise. If they know Cassandra, use it. If they're a Postgres shop, Citus is a pragmatic choice even if it's not theoretically optimal for the write pattern.
Good — I like that you considered organizational context. Let's talk about typing indicators and read receipts. These are high-frequency, low-value signals. How do you handle them?

Typing indicators are ephemeral — fire and forget. No persistence, no delivery guarantee. Send them through the NATS pub/sub path only. If it doesn't arrive, no one notices. We'd also debounce on the client — send 'typing' at most once every 3 seconds, and the recipient UI shows 'typing...' for 4 seconds before timing out. This keeps the volume manageable. Read receipts are slightly different — they should be persisted because users expect to see them later. But they're not time-critical like messages. I'd batch read receipt updates — when a user reads messages 45 through 60, send a single 'read up to 60' event rather than 16 individual receipts. Store the high-water mark per user per conversation.
In a 500-person group, read receipts become 500 * N events for N messages. That's a lot of state. Do you even show read receipts in large groups?

No — and this is what WhatsApp and Slack both do. Below a threshold — say 20 members — show individual read receipts. Above that, show aggregate: '47 members have read this' as a count, not individual indicators. For very large groups, don't show read receipts at all — just delivery confirmation. The storage model changes too: for small groups, store per-user-per-conversation high-water marks. For large groups, store only an aggregate counter that increments when members read. This caps the state at O(conversations) rather than O(users * conversations).
Let's close out. What would you build for v1 versus what you'd defer?

V1: WebSocket connections with long-polling fallback, 1:1 and group messaging through NATS for real-time delivery, Cassandra for message persistence, Redis for connection registry and sequence numbers, basic read receipts for small groups. I'd use a single region initially. Defer to v2: multi-region with conflict resolution, media messages (need an object store and upload/download service), message search (needs an Elasticsearch index), E2E encryption, large group optimizations, and the dual NATS+Kafka path — v1 can use Kafka alone if we accept slightly higher latency until we prove we need NATS.
Strong interview. You defended every decision well and were willing to revise when the argument was sound. That's exactly what I look for at the principal level. Thank you.

strengths: Defended every design choice with concrete technical reasoning when challenged
Willingly revised designs when presented with better arguments — shows intellectual flexibility
Excellent organizational awareness — considered team expertise when choosing technologies
weaknesses: Initial dual-write design with NATS+Kafka introduced unnecessary complexity that had to be walked back for v1
Capacity estimation could have been more thorough — didn't calculate message storage or network bandwidth
Didn't discuss media handling or search until prompted at the end
